features.name: Sharded Feature State
features.behavior: Split the mutable per-feature fields (state, evidence, owner, timestamps) out of feature_list.json into one file per feature under .harness/state/<id>.json, so two lanes landing different features never touch the same tracked path and merge without conflict by construction. feature_list.json keeps only declaration fields (id, name, behavior, dependencies, layers). verify-feature, session-trace, and harness-report read/write the shard files instead of rewriting the whole feature list.
features.verification: npm run check passes; verify-feature reads and writes only its own feature's shard file (never the shared feature_list.json); a simulated two-lane merge (two branches each updating a different feature's shard under .harness/state/) merges with zero conflicts; harness-report aggregates state correctly across all shards.

features.name: Upgrade Backups
features.behavior: Before harness-upgrade overwrites mustNotEdit CORE surfaces, snapshot the current on-disk state of every file about to be touched: checksum-deduped (skip a redundant backup when nothing changed), gzip-compressed per file, stored in .harness/backups/<id>/ (gitignored — a local safety net, not durable evidence). Retention keeps the 5 most recent unpinned backups; pinned backups are never pruned. backup-list/backup-pin/backup-unpin/backup-restore (restore accepts an id or "latest") round out the command surface. Restore is per file: existed=true writes the snapshotted content back, existed=false removes a file the operation newly created.
features.verification: npm run check passes; unit tests cover snapshot creation (including existed=false files), dedup, restore fidelity (including the existed=false removal case), and prune/pin interaction; the adoption matrix's upgrade test asserts a real upgrade() call creates a backup and that restoring it reproduces the pre-upgrade (corrupted) state before re-upgrading to leave the repo fixed.

features.name: Dogfooding Feedback Round 1
features.behavior: Three quick, low-risk fixes from real-world adopter feedback (DOGFOODING-FEEDBACK-payroll.md Tier 1), each tied to an incident that actually happened: (1) check-arch warns (does not fail) when untracked-but-not-gitignored files exist, since coverage rules like arch-005 only see git-tracked files and this caused two real CI breaks in an adopter project; (2) a new add-feature <id> <name> command appends a correctly-shaped, declaration-only feature stub, replacing the hand-rolled node -e JSON construction the adopter repeated 11+ times; (3) the lint layer fails on a duplicate or missing session number in PROGRESS.md's ### Session N headers (checked as a set, not file order, so a legitimate out-of-order hotfix write is not flagged) — the adopter's log accumulated a real duplicate session number that nothing ever caught.
features.verification: npm run check passes; unit tests cover the untracked-file warning (present/absent/no-git-repo), add-feature (stub shape, duplicate-id rejection, multi-word name handling), and the progress-log check (sequential, out-of-order-but-valid, duplicate, gap, no-sessions-yet cases).

features.name: Verification evidence is bound to committed code
features.behavior: verify-feature refuses to record passing evidence while the git working tree has uncommitted changes outside harness bookkeeping (.harness/state, .harness/logs, .harness/traces, .harness/trails, progress/, PROGRESS.md, progress.md, claude-progress.md, session-handoff.md), and fails if a layer leaves new changes there, so the recorded commit is exactly the code that passed. --allow-dirty records the evidence anyway, marked bound: false. Outside a git repository evidence is recorded with bound: false and a NOTE. Evidence also stores checksHash, a hash of the feature's declared layers (label, cmd, required); typecheck warns when a passing feature's layers changed after it was verified, and verify-feature treats a dependency with such stale evidence as unmet. Evidence recorded before this feature (no checksHash or bound field) stays valid.
features.verification: npm run check passes including new framework-check tests: dirty code refuses before any layer runs; bookkeeping-only changes do not; --allow-dirty records bound: false; a layer that writes a tracked or untracked file fails; outside git the evidence is bound: false; checksHash changes with label, cmd or required but not repair; typecheck warns on a stale passing feature and stays silent for legacy evidence; a dependency with stale evidence blocks verify-feature. npm run check-arch passes; this feature's own verify-feature runs on a clean, committed tree.

features.name: Upgrade dry run with a per-file plan
features.behavior: harness-upgrade <dir> --dry-run (and upgrade(root, { dryRun: true })) computes the full upgrade without writing anything: no file copied, no manifest rewrite, no instance file created, no .harness/backups snapshot. A real run applies exactly that plan. Unknown options fail.

features.name: Capture collection in verify-feature
features.behavior: A layer in feature_list.json may declare "captures": a list of globs (relative to the project root) naming the screenshots, videos or other artifacts the layer's command writes, such as test-results/**/*.png. After such a layer passes, verify-feature collects the files matching those globs that were written during this layer's run (modified at or after the layer started, so leftovers from earlier runs never count), copies them to .harness/logs/<feature>/captures/<NN>-<layer>/, adds captures: [{path, sha256, bytes}] to that layer's evidence entry, and prints each copied path with the instruction to open it and compare it to the feature's declared behavior. A layer that declares captures but produces none fails, like a required layer that reports only SKIP. When a capture source folder is not gitignored, the existing uncommitted-changes failure after the layers names that folder and says to ignore it. typecheck rejects captures that are not a non-empty list of non-empty strings. A layer's captures count toward the feature's checksHash only when declared, so existing evidence does not go stale. Layers without captures behave exactly as before. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/USAGE.md and its template describe the field.

features.name: README stays current with the app
features.behavior: A feature passing the gate is the harness's significant change. clean-check fails while README.md has not changed since the most recent gate-verified feature passed: README.md must be changed in that feature's verified commit or a later one, or have uncommitted changes. A feature whose users see no change declares "readme": "<reason>" in feature_list.json and is skipped (typecheck rejects an empty or non-string value); the check then applies to the latest verified feature without that field. When the history cannot tell (a commit missing from a shallow clone), it warns instead of failing. The same rule runs in this repository and in every adopter: README.md describes the app being built — what it does, how to run it, what a user can do now — not the harness. AGENTS.md gains a MUST rule enforced by clean-check, its End of Session steps and the update-docs and session-handoff skills say what to write, the adopter README template gains a 'What It Does Now' section, docs/USAGE.md and its template document the rule, and a decision record explains it.
features.verification: Runner tests in a temporary git repository: clean-check fails when README.md last changed before the latest verified feature's commit, passes when it changed in that commit, a later one or the working tree, skips a feature that declares readme and checks the previous one, and warns when the evidence commit is unknown; typecheck rejects a malformed readme field; this repository passes after the feature's own README update; npm run check passes; verify-feature runs on a committed tree.

features.name: README contrasted with the repository
features.behavior: lint checks README.md against a conventional structure and against the repository, the same in this repository and in every adopter. Structure, based on the Standard Readme convention: exactly one level-1 title, a short description before the first section, an install section (Install, Installation, Getting Started, Quick Start or Setup), a usage section (Usage, Examples, How to Use, How It Works or What It/the <name> Does), a License section, and a Table of Contents section when the README is longer than 100 lines. Claims, so the README says nothing the repository does not do: every npm, pnpm or yarn script it runs and every make target in its code exists, every relative link points to an existing file, and every repository path in its inline code exists; HTML comments, external links and placeholders (angle brackets, wildcards, braces, NNN or YYYY) are skipped. Each problem is reported with its line number. What a mechanical check cannot judge, a shipped readme-review skill covers: every capability the README claims has evidence in the code, tests or a passing feature, and every capability users can see appears in the README or a document it links, written about the app being built in the present tense. clean-check's README failure (feat-051) points to the skill. This repository's README is brought in line by that review, the adopter README template passes the check, and USAGE (both copies), AGENTS.md's skills list and a decision record describe it.
features.verification: Runner tests: lint:readme passes a conventional README; it fails, with line numbers, a missing title, description, install, usage or license section, a long README without contents, an unknown npm script or make target, a missing link target and a missing inline path, and ignores HTML comments, external links and placeholders; this repository's README and the adopter template pass; the readme-review skill is validated by lint and shipped by harness-upgrade; npm run check passes; verify-feature runs on a committed tree.

features.name: README command claims come only from shell fences
features.behavior: lint:readme (feat-052) takes npm, pnpm and yarn script claims and make target claims from inline code spans and from fenced code blocks whose info string is a shell language (bash, sh, shell, zsh, console, shell-session, powershell, ps1, pwsh, cmd, bat; first word, any case) or that have no info string. A fence tagged with any other language (text, json, yaml, ts, ...) is sample output or source, not a command, so prose in it such as 'make the calls explicit' is not reported as a missing make target. Shell comments in a shell fence are still not commands. Repository path claims stay what they were: only inline code in prose is checked, never fenced code of any language. docs/USAGE.md and its template say which fences are read as commands, and a decision record explains the choice.
features.verification: Runner tests: a text fence with 'make the ...' and 'npm run nothing' passes lint:readme; a bash fence with a missing make target still fails with its line; an untagged fence still counts; npm run check passes; verify-feature runs on a committed tree.

features.name: Clarify a feature before activating it
features.behavior: Before a feature is activated, its declaration is checked for ambiguity and every open question is answered and recorded. npm run clarify -- <id> prints the feature behavior, verification and dependencies, then a fixed checklist of questions (terms the behavior uses but does not define, inputs and edge cases it does not cover, error cases, files and docs it will touch, whether each sentence of the behavior is covered by the verification text) and flags it finds mechanically: vague words (etc, appropriately, properly, as needed, should handle, TBD, TODO), a verification that names no test or command, and a behavior sentence with no counterpart in the verification. The agent answers each question from the repository and its docs, citing the file, or asks the human; npm run clarify -- <id> --record <file> stores the answers as clarifications in .harness/state/<id>.json, each with question, answer and source (a repository path or the word human), or the single entry none when nothing was open. npm run activate -- <id> refuses a feature with no clarifications recorded and names the clarify command; --skip-clarify activates anyway and records clarifications: skipped, which the session brief shows. A clarification that changes what done means is not written into the answers: the agent stops and asks for the behavior in feature_list.json to be edited first. A shipped clarify skill describes the step, feature-cycle, AGENTS.md (startup and working rules), docs/USAGE.md and its template describe it, harness-upgrade ships the skill and the command to adopters, and a decision record explains why the step exists (adapted from the clarify step of spec-driven development) and why it records answers instead of rewriting the declaration.
features.verification: Runner tests: clarify prints the checklist and flags vague words, a verification without a test or command, and an uncovered behavior sentence; clarify --record writes clarifications to the state shard and rejects entries without question, answer or source; activate refuses an unclarified feature with a message naming clarify, accepts one with clarifications or none, and with --skip-clarify records skipped; the brief shows a skipped clarification; lint validates the clarify skill and harness-upgrade ships it; npm run check passes; verify-feature runs on a committed tree.

features.name: Pull requests carry evidence for the commit they merge
features.behavior: npm run evidence-check (and its make mirror) compares the branch with its base (the merge-base with the default branch, or --base <ref>) and finds every feature whose state shard became passing on the branch. For each, the commit named in its evidence must be an ancestor of HEAD, and every file changed between that commit and HEAD must be harness bookkeeping: .harness/state/, .harness/trails/, progress/, PROGRESS.md, README.md and docs/quality-document.md. Otherwise it fails, naming the feature, its evidence commit and each non-bookkeeping file that changed after it, and says to rerun verify-feature. A branch that passes no feature reports so and passes. The shipped CI workflow and the adopter CI template run it on pull requests, so a pull request whose code changed after verification cannot go green. docs/USAGE.md and its template describe the command, AGENTS.md names it as the gate behind the MUST about committing before verify-feature, and a decision record explains why the check runs at the pull request rather than only at verify time.
features.verification: Runner tests in throwaway repositories: a branch whose feature passed on its last code commit passes evidence-check; a code edit committed after the evidence commit fails, naming the feature and the file; a progress note or state shard committed after it still passes; an evidence commit that is not an ancestor of HEAD fails; a branch with no newly passing feature passes; --base selects the base. Lint confirms both CI workflows run evidence-check on pull requests. npm run check passes; verify-feature runs on a committed tree.

features.name: Checks scoped to what the change touched
features.behavior: npm run check classifies the files changed against the merge-base with the default branch, plus uncommitted and untracked files. When every changed file is documentation (a .md file outside skills/ and templates/, or a file under docs/), it runs only the lint layer, which already validates the progress log, the README and skills, and reports each other layer as SKIP with the reason docs-only change; those skips never count as PASS. Any other changed file, no detectable base, or --full runs every layer as today. The classification and the layers it ran are printed before the first layer. verify-feature, CI on the default branch and the adopter CI template always run the full chain. docs/USAGE.md, docs/HARNESS.md and their templates describe the scoping and --full, and a decision record explains why only documentation is scoped.
features.verification: Runner tests in throwaway repositories: a change to README.md alone runs lint and reports the other layers as SKIP with the docs-only reason; a change to a script plus a .md file runs every layer; a change to a SKILL.md runs every layer; --full runs every layer on a docs-only change; a repository with no default-branch base runs every layer; verify-feature still runs every declared layer on a docs-only change. npm run check passes; verify-feature runs on a committed tree.

features.name: Lanes get their own ports and environment
features.behavior: npm run lane-new -- <id> reserves a block of 10 ports for the lane in a registry kept in the repository's common git directory, so every worktree of the clone sees it, and writes .env.lane at the lane root with HARNESS_LANE=<id>, HARNESS_PORT_BASE=<first port> and HARNESS_DB_SUFFIX=_<id with dashes replaced by underscores>. Blocks start at the port given by lanePortBase in .harness/manifest.json (default 4100) and never overlap a block held by another lane. If the main checkout has a .env that git ignores there, it is copied into the lane once and left for the lane to change; a .env git would track is not copied, and lane-new says so, so secrets never become an untracked file a commit could pick up. lane-list shows each lane's port block; lane-land and lane-drop release the block; a block whose lane branch no longer exists is released by the next lane-new. .env.lane is excluded through the repository's common info/exclude file, so it is ignored in every worktree without editing the project's .gitignore. docs/USAGE.md, the parallel-lanes skill and their templates say how a project's dev server and database read these variables, and a decision record explains the registry location.
features.verification: Runner tests in throwaway repositories: two lanes get non-overlapping port blocks starting at the default base; lanePortBase changes the start; .env.lane holds the three variables; an ignored main-checkout .env is copied, a tracked-or-unignored one is not (with a message), and a missing one is not created; lane-list prints the blocks; lane-drop and lane-land release a block so the next lane reuses it; a block whose branch was deleted by hand is reclaimed; .env.lane is not tracked by git. npm run check passes; verify-feature runs on a committed tree.

features.name: Opt-in push and commit-message hooks
features.behavior: npm run hooks-install installs, next to the existing pre-commit hook, a pre-push hook that refuses a push to the repository's default branch (read from origin/HEAD, else master or main), naming the branch and saying to push a feature branch and open a pull request; setting HARNESS_ALLOW_DEFAULT_PUSH=1 for that push lets it through and the hook says so. It also installs a commit-msg hook that applies rules declared in .harness/commit-rules.json: subjectPattern (a regular expression the first line must match), maxSubjectLength, and forbid (patterns no line may contain), each failure naming the rule and the offending line. Messages that git generates for merges and reverts are accepted. The file ships disabled, so the commit-msg hook accepts everything until a project enables it, and lint validates the file's shape. hooks-uninstall removes both hooks; existing hooks are never replaced. docs/USAGE.md, docs/HARNESS.md, AGENTS.md and their templates describe the hooks, harness-upgrade ships them, and a decision record explains why the push rule has an explicit override.
features.verification: Runner tests in throwaway repositories with a bare remote: a push to the default branch is refused with the branch named; a push to another branch succeeds; HARNESS_ALLOW_DEFAULT_PUSH=1 lets a default-branch push through; with commit rules enabled, a subject that misses subjectPattern, one over maxSubjectLength and a message containing a forbid pattern are each refused naming the rule, and a git merge message is accepted; with rules disabled every message is accepted; lint rejects a malformed commit-rules file; hooks-uninstall removes both hooks; an existing hook is left in place. npm run check passes; verify-feature runs on a committed tree.

features.name: Skill usage report
features.behavior: Session notes created by progress-new gain a Skills used section listing the names of the skills loaded in that session, or none. Notes written before the section existed are skipped and counted separately. npm run report includes the same table. docs/USAGE.md, docs/HARNESS.md, the session-handoff and write-skill skills and their templates describe the section and the command, and a decision record explains why usage is recorded by the agent in the note instead of read from tool logs.
